title_r: Conceptual Replication of Four Key Findings about Factual Corrections and Misinformation during the 2020 US Election: Evidence from Panel-Survey Experiments
abstract_r: Abstract In the final two months of the 2020 US election, we conducted eight panel experiments to evaluate the immediate and medium-term effects of misinformation and factual corrections. Our results corroborate four sets of existing findings: fact-checks reliably improve factual accuracy, while misinformation degrades it; effects of fact-checks on belief accuracy endure, though they fade with time; effects on attitudes are minuscule; and there are important partisan asymmetries. We also offer one new empirical finding suggesting that effect heterogeneities by personality type and cognitive style may reflect attention paid to treatments. Our study confirms that the fundamental push and pull of misinformation and factual corrections on political beliefs holds even in electoral settings as saturated with mistruths as the 2020 US election.

title_r: Pre-test of product perception for the replication attempt of the study by Sela et al. (2009)
abstract_r: As part of the attempt to replicate the study by Sela et al. investigating the effect of assortment size on option choice, we conduct a pre-test to show that the stimulus material chosen is appropriate. Participants will see six printers and six Bluetooth speakers and are asked to indicate whether they perceive the products as utilitarian or hedonic. We also check whether one of the products is preferred within its category. We expect that printers will be perceived as more utilitarian than Bluetooth speakers and Bluetooth speakers as more hedonic than printers and that none of the options will be preferred within its own category.
